I've been working this land in Quzhou for over half a century. I know what this soil does, what the weather brings, and what my body can handle at 73. My wife and I can't put in the hours we used to, so I think carefully about where to spend my labor.

My 12 mu divides naturally: I'll keep 8 mu in the wheat-maize rotation — that's my backbone, mechanizable, predictable — and the remaining 4 mu goes to cotton. Cotton is getting harder. It demands hand labor at topping and picking, but the price is still worth it and I know the crop intimately. I won't give it up yet.

For **wheat**, I'll use an improved certified variety from the county seed station — I stopped saving my own seed fifteen years ago when yields climbed after switching. I'll rotary till after maize harvest in October, apply base fertilizer, then split the nitrogen: base plus topdressing at jointing. Four irrigations: pre-winter, turning green, jointing, and heading. Herbicide once, fungicide once for powdery mildew. Straightforward.

For **maize**, I go straight in after wheat harvest with no-tillage and a hybrid seed —郑单958 or similar. Summer heat does the work. Three irrigations, two pesticide passes. Nitrogen goes in at planting and again at big bell stage.

For **cotton**, I plough in spring, plant hybrid seed with plastic mulch. Cotton needs more water and far more pesticide attention — bollworm, aphids, spider mites. Five irrigations spread through the season, seven pesticide applications. I top it myself in July. It's the hardest work on my calendar but I've done it so many times my hands know what to do.
